meta.note: All figures provisional and subject to revision by the issuing statistical office.

markets.name: United Kingdom
markets.commentary: Second rise in a row, to 3.1% from 2.9%, and 0.5% in the single month. Transport did almost all of it: the division went from 3.6% to 4.6% and motor fuels are 23.0% higher than a year ago. Petrol reached 161.3 pence a litre, the highest since November 2022, after a 9.1 pence jump in the month. Core stayed at 2.6% for a third month and services stayed at 3.4%, so the underlying picture has not moved at all. What has changed is the pipeline. Last month factory gate prices were cooling; this month output prices rose 0.7% and the annual rate went to 3.7% from a revised 3.3%, driven by coke and refined petroleum products up 8.6% in the month and 49.1% over the year. Input prices also turned up, to 6.1% from 5.8%. ONS flags that both series are still being distorted by the Middle East conflict, and July was revised substantially.

markets.name: Euro Area
markets.commentary: Up to 3.2% from 2.9%, the highest since May, and revised down a tenth from the 3.3% flash. Energy is the whole story: 14.3% year on year against 10.3% in July, and 2.9% in the single month, contributing 1.29 points of the 3.2%. Everything else went the other way. Core (excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) fell to 2.4% from 2.5% and services dropped to 3.0% from 3.3%, flat on the month. Food, alcohol and tobacco slipped again to 1.1%. The one exception is non-energy industrial goods, up to 1.2% from 0.9%, which is the first sign of energy costs reaching goods prices. July producer prices, the latest published, jumped 1.6% on the month and the annual rate went back up to 5.8% from 4.6% in June, so the pipeline that was cooling last month is refilling.

markets.name: United States
markets.commentary: The monthly number looks bad and the annual one does not. Headline rose 0.4% in August after 0.1% in July, but the annual rate held at 3.4%. Gasoline was up 3.9% and accounted for more than a third of the monthly rise; energy overall rose 2.1% and is 16.3% higher than a year ago. Core rose 0.3% on the month yet the annual core rate fell again, to 2.4% from 2.5%, and is now the lowest core reading in this set apart from France and Italy. Shelter picked up to 0.3% after 0.1%. Airline fares are still the outlier, up 2.7% in the month and 23.4% over the year. The producer side is the thing to watch: PPI final demand rose 0.4% and the annual rate jumped to 5.4% from 4.7%, with final demand energy up 4.2% and diesel up 24.1% in a single month.

markets.name: Japan
markets.commentary: The run of increases stopped. Headline held at 1.9% and the measure excluding fresh food and energy held at 1.9%. The narrower measure excluding fresh food only fell back to 1.7% from 1.8%, missing the consensus for no change and leaving it under the Bank of Japan's 2% target for an eighth month. On the producer side CGPI fell 0.2% in the month and eased to 7.6% from 7.7%, with electricity and gas down 2.2% and petroleum and coal products down 1.7%. The bigger move is imports: yen-basis import prices came down to 24.8% year on year from 29.3%, and crude petroleum was the single largest contributor to the fall. That is the first real relief on the cost side in five months. The producer-to-consumer gap is 5.7 points, still by far the widest of the four, but it is now closing from the top rather than waiting for CPI to catch up. Monthly CPI rates are not published on a seasonally adjusted basis, hence n/a.

euroMembers.name: Germany
euroMembers.note: HICP edged up to 2.9% from 2.8%. Energy accelerated again to 10.5% from 8.3%, the biggest annual rise in over three years, with motor fuels 27.7% dearer than a year ago and still rising 3.1% in the month despite the fuel discount having ended back in June. Heating oil is up 49.6%. Household energy as a whole is actually 0.7% cheaper than a year ago because electricity (-5.5%) and gas (-2.9%) are held down by federal measures. Core unchanged at 2.4% and services slowed to 2.8%, so the domestic picture is stable. Producer prices for July rose to 3.1% from 1.9% in June and are now above consumer prices again.

euroMembers.name: France
euroMembers.note: HICP to 2.6% from 2.4%, national CPI to 2.4% from 2.1%. Energy accelerated for a third month, to 16.7% from 12.6%, with petroleum products at 28.7% and diesel at 36.4%. Against that, core fell to 1.1% from 1.3% and services slowed to 1.9% from 2.2%, held down by accommodation prices collapsing to 0.7% from 7.3%. France has the softest underlying inflation of the four by a wide margin and the widest gap between headline and core. Producer prices for July at 3.4%.

euroMembers.name: Italy
euroMembers.note: Caution on the Italian headline this month: Eurostat's final release puts HICP at 3.2% year on year and +0.1% on the month, while Istat's own release of the same date reports HICP at 2.9% and +1.0%. The two do not reconcile, so the figures here are Eurostat's for comparability with the other three and should be treated as provisional. On the national NIC index, which is not in dispute, inflation went to 3.3% from 2.9% and core eased to 1.5% from 1.6%. Energy is doing all the work: regulated products from 14.8% to 18.6% and non-regulated from 11.4% to 17.0%. Producer prices for July are the hottest of the four at 9.3%, up from 6.8% in June.

euroMembers.name: Spain
euroMembers.note: Still the highest of the four and pulling away. HICP jumped seven tenths to 4.6% and the national CPI to 4.3%, the highest since February 2023. Transport rose more than three points to 9.5%, the highest since August 2022, on fuels and lubricants that were falling in August 2025. Food and non-alcoholic beverages added to it, up to 2.3% from 1.6%. Core actually eased a tenth to 2.9%, which is the one piece of good news, though it remains the highest core of the four. Producer prices for July at 9.3%, up from 7.0% in June, level with Italy.

euroMembersNote: Headline HICP year on year and month on month are both shown on the comparable Eurostat basis (final August 2026 release, published 17 September). Note that Istat's national release reports a different August HICP for Italy (2.9% year on year, +1.0% on the month) than Eurostat does; Eurostat's figure is used here for comparability and the Italian headline should be treated as provisional this month. Core measures come from each national office and are not identical: Germany is CPI excluding food and energy, France is INSEE underlying inflation, Italy is NIC excluding energy and unprocessed food, Spain is CPI excluding unprocessed food and energy. PPI is held at July 2026 for all four so it stays comparable with the euro area aggregate (+5.8%), which is the latest published month; the August euro area figure is due 5 October. On that July basis: Germany +3.1%, France +3.4%, Italy +9.3%, Spain +9.3%.

signals.title: The energy shock is now in every market, not just Europe
signals.observe: Last month the US was falling while Europe rose. In August all four moved the same way. Euro area energy is 14.3% year on year and rose 2.9% in the month. UK motor fuels are 23.0% higher over the year and petrol hit 161.3 pence a litre, the highest since November 2022. German energy is 10.5%, the biggest rise in over three years, and French energy 16.7%. US energy rose 2.1% in the month, with gasoline up 3.9% accounting for over a third of the entire monthly CPI increase.
signals.why: This is the Iran conflict feeding through to crude and refined product prices everywhere at once, which is why the timing is synchronised. It is no longer a story about European policy support being withdrawn; Germany's fuel discount ended three months ago and the US has no equivalent measure at all.
signals.action: Any Q4 or 2027 budgeting for fuel, freight, or energy-linked input costs should be built off August levels across all markets, not the June trough. The previous assumption that the US would stay decoupled no longer holds.

signals.title: Core is falling in almost every market where the headline is rising
signals.observe: Euro area core fell to 2.4% from 2.5% and services to 3.0% from 3.3%. US core fell to 2.4% from 2.5%. France fell to 1.1% from 1.3% and Italy to 1.5% from 1.6%. Spain eased to 2.9% from 3.0%. The UK and Germany were unchanged, at 2.6% and 2.4%. Not one of the seven core measures in this file went up.
signals.why: The headline moves are a relative price shock in one component, not a broad-based rise in the cost of doing business. Services inflation, which is the closest available proxy for labour costs, decelerated in the euro area, France and Germany and was flat in the UK.
signals.action: When the August headline prints get used internally to argue for price increases or cost-of-living adjustments, the counter is on this row of the dashboard. Every core and services measure is flat or down. The case for repricing on underlying cost pressure is weaker than it was in June.

signals.title: Western producer prices have turned back up just as Japan's finally cool
signals.observe: Euro area PPI went from 4.6% to 5.8% and rose 1.6% in the month, the sharpest monthly rise since March. UK output prices went from 3.3% to 3.7% and input prices from 5.8% to 6.1%. US final demand went from 4.7% to 5.4%. Japan moved the other way: CGPI fell 0.2% in the month to 7.6% from 7.7%, and yen-basis import prices dropped to 24.8% from 29.3%.
signals.why: Producer prices pick up crude and refined products faster and at higher weight than consumer baskets do, so the Western pipeline is absorbing the oil move now and will pass some of it on over the next two quarters. Japan's move is a currency and crude effect running in reverse after five months of escalation.
signals.action: The producer-to-consumer gap is Japan 5.7 points, euro area 2.6, US 2.0, UK 0.6. Japan is still the one to price conservatively, but the direction has changed: assume the gap closes by CGPI falling rather than CPI rising. For Europe and the US, assume some of the August producer jump reaches consumer prices in Q4.
